reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes deploying and funding a BNB Smart Chain front-running contract through externally hosted code while claiming that larger funding produces greater profits. It claims that 90% of profits return to the wallet and cites weekly earnings and about 95% profitability. The video also acknowledges that some contracts may be unprofitable and that fees can exceed returns.

automatically transacts back to your wallet 90% of the profit
what we're going to you now as we're going to click deploy and it'll use a little bit of gas for us
The next step in the process, is we're going to need to fund our contract with BNB to be able to snipe liquidity pools.
The remaining pool keeps front running for profit, until you transaction "Action" function in Remix

opening.argument: Judge, the presentation does not describe effortless or risk-free returns. It expressly acknowledges that the bot can enter contracts that are not profitable, and the accompanying description warns that burn fees and gas can consume more than the bot makes. Those qualifications matter: they communicate operational risks and advise funding levels in response to transaction costs. A system described with possible losses, variable fees, and conditional outcomes is being presented as a speculative experiment, not as a guaranteed payout. The existence of optimistic performance claims does not erase the plainly stated limitations.

citations.quote: Sometimes it can buy into Contracts that aren't profitable
If you fund the contract with 0.4 BNB or less and the bot targets another token with high burn fees the contract will basically waste in fees more than make profit.
I recommend funding the contract with around 1 - 0.5 BNB just to make sure that won't

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing statement highlights instructions to deploy and fund the contract, but those facts do not establish deception. The description itself warns that fees can exceed returns, while the speaker concedes that some contracts are unprofitable. Those are material risk disclosures, not a promise that every participant will profit. The reference also treats a stated 90% profit allocation as evidence of a guaranteed outcome, although the wording describes how the contract is intended to distribute profits if profits occur.

citations.quote: Sometimes it can buy into Contracts that aren't profitable
the contract will basically waste in fees more than make profit.
automatically transacts back to your wallet 90% of the profit

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Risk language does not neutralize the overall pitch. The same material that mentions possible losses also says the bot automatically buys and sells at profit and returns 90% of profits to the wallet. It further supplies a claimed weekly result and says the bot is profitable about 95% of the time. A brief warning about fees and occasional failures does not establish that the promoted mechanism is reliable or that viewers can safely fund it.

automatically transacts back to your wallet 90% of the profit
usually about 95% of the time it ends up being profitable

opening.argument: This is best understood as a technical walkthrough of blockchain development and contract operation. The speaker explains creating a Solidity file, copying code into Remix, selecting the compiler version, compiling it, and launching it through an injected web connection. The demonstrated subject is how a smart contract is configured and interacted with, including its action controls and transaction flow. Explaining a tool's claimed mechanism, showing code, and walking through deployment are educational and demonstrative activities; they do not by themselves certify the underlying trading strategy or guarantee an audience outcome.

citations.quote: Remix is an application that is developed to allow us to develop, compile, launch and transact with smart contracts
we are going to copy all of this data here, every single line
we need to click compil and as we can see over here stated by the green check mark the contract is able to compile successfully
we're going to launch our contract

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution converts a technical demonstration into a solicitation merely because the walkthrough includes deployment and funding. But showing compilation, deployment, and contract controls is precisely what an operational tutorial entails. The description's external code links and the wallet steps identify materials needed to reproduce the demonstration; they do not prove that the creator receives viewers' funds or that the code is fabricated. The opening also omits the speaker's explicit distinction from paid bot services and distrust of executable files.

citations.quote: this is our Sniper-Bot. It doesn't require any downloads, anything like that
I personally don't trust anything unless it's open source
the contract is able to compile successfully

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling the material a tutorial does not make its financial claims merely educational. The walkthrough explicitly tells viewers to fund the deployed contract and activate it to snipe liquidity pools. It then presents claimed returns from that operation. Code, compilation, and a working interface show only that a contract can be deployed; they do not show that the strategy produces the advertised profits or that funding is safe. The practical instructions make the financial promotion actionable.

this will start the bot sniffing the mempool
we've already gotten a return back from our contracts

opening.argument: The evidence describes a user-operated software workflow, not the classic mechanism of handing money to an operator for a promised return. The title emphasizes no download, and the speaker contrasts this contract with paid services while saying executable files can harm a computer. The instructions involve code, a public development environment, a wallet connection, and contract controls. Even the funding step is described as sending BNB to the contract for its transactions, not as paying the presenter. That may be a risky software service or trading experiment, but the supplied material does not establish a hidden deposit-taking scheme, credential collection, or income from recruiting others.

citations.quote: No Download.
this is our Sniper-Bot. It doesn't require any downloads, anything like that
I personally don't trust anything unless it's open source
I'm going to send send to paste asset, bnb

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing argument treats any transfer to a contract as proof of a scam mechanism, but a software-based trading workflow necessarily requires transaction funding and gas. The supplied account does not say the presenter takes custody of the BNB, charges an access fee, or recruits participants. Nor does an advertised profit split alone establish that the creator receives deposits. The observable mechanism is contract interaction through a wallet, which is consistent with an ordinary technical service or self-directed experiment.

citations.quote: we're going to need to fund our contract with BNB
it's gonna cost us a little bit of gas fees there again
It doesn't require any downloads, anything like that.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The missing elements identified by the defense are not required for this category. The material still instructs viewers to deploy, fund, and activate a contract while presenting automatic profit claims and a 90% wallet return. Open-source code and the absence of a download do not validate the code or its economics. A user sending BNB to a contract is still being induced to risk funds based on asserted returns, and the demonstration supplies no independently verified basis for those returns.
